analysis.one_liner: Lets governors veto endangered species protections in their states and pays landowners for lost property value.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2017 with one sponsor and seven Republican cosponsors, then never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act so that a species could not be listed as endangered or threatened in any state without that state governor's consent. Every federal list of protected species would need a fresh act of Congress to take effect, and species would come off the list automatically after five years. Citizens could no longer petition to add or remove species, and environmental groups would lose the attorney fees that let them sue to enforce the law. Landowners could get a guaranteed approval of a proposed land use if the Interior Department misses a 90-day deadline, and 150% of their property's value if a protection lowers it.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and developers of land that harbors endangered species habitat, and industries such as utilities and construction that face costs when a listing restricts building, logging, or water projects. A governor could take over management of any species found only in that state, with no judicial review of that decision, and could simply decline to protect it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Landowners, developers, and utilities facing species restrictions

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal agencies to obtain the consent of each governor before listing a species as endangered or threatened in that state [S2].
Provides that owners or lessees of property can get a determination on a proposed land use, and the use is deemed compliant if Interior fails to respond within 90 days [S2].
Allows owners or lessees to seek monetary compensation — 150% of fair market value — when a Fish and Wildlife Service action cuts their property's value by 50% or more for its intended use [S3].
Lets a governor claim exclusive authority to manage any species found only within that state, including over federal public lands, with no judicial review of the state's actions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public. Protections for endangered species would depend on the agreement of every governor with the species in its range and on Congress repeatedly voting to re-approve lists. Taxpayers would fund the 150% compensation payments to landowners. Public lands could be managed under state law for species a governor deems intrastate, and citizens would lose their standing to petition for listings or recover attorney fees in enforcement suits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and everyone who values species protection

drawbacks.text: Species would be automatically removed from the list after five years, and relisting would require a new act of Congress, so protection would lapse whenever Congress does not act [S2].

Interested persons could no longer petition to add or remove species, and awards of attorney fees in citizen suits would be eliminated, removing the main tools private citizens have used to enforce the Act [S2].

A 90-day deadline that deems any proposed land use compliant if Interior does not answer, and a 150% compensation requirement, would make the program costly for taxpayers and could discourage protective determinations [S3].
State management of intrastate species would not be subject to judicial review in any federal or state court, so a governor's decision not to protect a species could not be challenged [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal is to address landowner burdens under the Endangered Species Act, and guaranteeing answers to land-use questions is a legitimate aim. But the bill goes far past that: it effectively gives each governor a veto over federal listings, sunsets every listing after five years, removes citizens' petitions and lawsuits, and pays landowners 150% of property value for regulatory losses. The cost of that combination falls on species protection and on taxpayers, and the bill received no action in committee, so Congress never weighed the trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which never held a markup or brought it to the floor, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer of Missouri introduced the Endangered Species Management Self-Determination Act on April 25, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1].
Seven Republican representatives cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].

The full action history shows only two actions: introduction and referral to committee, with no hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action recorded before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing Endangered Species Act, with its citizen petitions, citizen suits, and court review, remained in force. The landowners, developers, and utilities the bill was written for gained nothing, and no species protections were weakened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public's existing species protections were untouched

for.name: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let governors veto species listings, require congressional approval of the protected lists, and pay landowners for regulatory losses.

for.name: Rep. Pete Sessions
for.what_they_did: Joined Luetkemeyer in introducing the bill on April 25, 2017.

for.name: 7 Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill after its introduction.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or a vote, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support on record, and no vote ever took place.

industries.industry: Landowners and real estate developers with species habitat on their land
industries.note: The bill would have given them deemed approvals after 90 days and 150% compensation for value lost to species protections, and let governors take over species regulation with no court review. Because the bill died, none of these benefits materialized.

industries.industry: Electric power and water project operators (federal power administrations and their customers)
industries.note: The bill would have weakened listing restrictions that constrain dams and transmission, but it also would have required the Bonneville, Southeastern, Southwestern, and Western power administrations to bill customers monthly for the share of ESA compliance costs — an accountability measure aimed at making species rules look expensive. Neither side took effect.

industries.industry: Environmental and conservation groups that litigate under the ESA
industries.note: The bill would have stripped attorney-fee awards in citizen suits and barred citizens from petitioning to list species, removing their main enforcement tools. The bill's death keeps those tools in place.

industries.industry: Timber, mining, and construction interests reliant on weaker species rules
industries.note: The bill's findings describe ESA listings as a tool that halts infrastructure projects, and its state-veto and compensation mechanisms would have eased those constraints. Nothing in it became law.
